extracted.intended_audience: administrators and administrative analysts (esp. in government agencies)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, distributing, timing, and measuring administrative work within and between organizational units, with emphasis on avoiding excessive functionalism and administrative bottlenecks. Covers principles for assigning tasks, choosing what to centralize, and methods for time/work-unit analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Each task should contribute positively to the basic purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Each task should contribute positively to the basic purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a criterion when analyzing tasks; eliminate or reassign tasks that do not advance the organization's primary objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine similar tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Similar tasks should be combined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group like activities to increase efficiency and reduce duplication; consider combinations when mapping functions and sub-functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize administrative moves
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative moves should be as few and short as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design sequences and channels to reduce the number and length of administrative steps (fewer handoffs, streamlined routing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance each task
rubrics_metrics.description: Each task should be well-balanced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign tasks so that workload, difficulty, and required skills are appropriately matched to individuals/units to avoid over- or under-assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide work by organization's major purposes (line functions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic division of administrative work should be according to the organization's major purposes (line functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational structure and major units should map to line functions; staff functions common to several line functions may be centralized only if they improve quality and ease line work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure staff divisions do not obstruct line work
rubrics_metrics.description: Staff divisions must not be allowed to obstruct the work of line divisions, nor should their technical controls go out of bounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retain staff advisory/coordinative roles; avoid staff controls that cause delays, irrelevant standards, or loss of line authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align responsibility with authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Responsibility and authority for performance should not be separated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an executive is held responsible for action, they must also have the power to act without awaiting approval from a non-responsible control agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep administrative sequences short
rubrics_metrics.description: Work assignments should allow as short administrative sequences as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short sequences improve speed and clarity; differentiation of fields should proceed from function and project rather than from specific sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider qualitative and quantitative capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualitative and quantitative capacity should be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign functions, sub-functions, and tasks within known abilities and skills; do not give individuals a regular volume of work they cannot dispatch promptly without overworking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use measurable work units and common denominators
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be constant search for the measurable elements in tasks, and work units should be applied as widely as practical; reduce different basic units to a common denominator such as the work-hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop units for common operations (transcribing, typing, filing, auditing vouchers) and convert to man-hours for budgeting and scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equalize workloads on objective bases
rubrics_metrics.description: So far as possible, work loads within a unit should be equalized according to objective bases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use measurement, work-unit standards, or objective criteria to balance assignments across individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance direct administrative channels with specialist use
rubrics_metrics.description: In distributing work between units a balance must be struck between seeking the most direct channels of administration (fewest moves) and using the skill and experience of specialists as effectively as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For undertakings with many technical phases, compromise so the product is sound without procedures becoming too complicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place specialists to keep recurrent projects within major divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An organization's specialists should be so placed that its various types of recurrent projects can be kept within major divisions as far as possible and interdivisional contacts will be mostly on policy rather than detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept some apparent duplication of function if consolidation would complicate operating procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid over-consolidation of staff operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Consolidation of staff operations such as purchasing, personnel, and accounting, if carried too far, increases the volume of detailed interdivisional contact and can hamper administration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where centralization hampers line operations, allow centralized staff agencies to act mainly as advisers and coordinators and decentralize detailed operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not functionalize administration excessively
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme functionalism — concentrating all processes within staff divisions while reducing line divisions to coordinators — is detrimental because it multiplies moves, obscures responsibility, and may substitute irrelevant process standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of adopting manufacturing-style functionalism wholesale in administrative contexts; preserve line authority and subject-matter purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralize only activities with standard techniques and little subject-matter relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities most advantageously centralized are those least related to the specific subject matter and having standard techniques applicable to any field of activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: purchasing of common items (not specialized apparatus), personnel work (except recruitment/final appraisal of specialists), office services, duplicating, photography (unless subject knowledge needed), building management, transportation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not centralize activities not susceptible to centralization
rubrics_metrics.description: Activities not susceptible to centralization include technical research and planning (except management planning), engineering, most clerical work (particularly when clerks are potential executives), and management of labor forces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These activities require subject-matter knowledge and are best kept near line units to preserve purpose and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use reserve personnel pools to handle peak loads
rubrics_metrics.description: To minimize waste of time caused by slack periods without extreme functionalism, give each unit enough personnel for normal volume and handle peak loads with a reserve force or 'pool' of clerks, statisticians, research workers, executives, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reserve pool can also serve as a training ground for new employees and those being groomed for advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operate personnel exchange services with unit production charts
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a personnel exchange service to loan employees between units for brief periods, using weekly 'unit production charts' indicating how many employee hours of each class/grade might be wished for during the ensuing week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure lending does not jeopardize security of tenure; operate interchangeably with the reserve force and coordinate with personnel/management planning offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign tasks to lowest level consistent with proper performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Tasks should be assigned to the lowest levels consistent with proper performance; failure to recognize this leads to 'administrative bottlenecks.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid undue concentration of executive authority; empower lower levels to act when appropriate to prevent traffic-jam-like delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for administrative bottlenecks
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two ways of dealing with administrative bottlenecks: widen them by dividing the work among a sufficient number of officials, or re-route business around them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze causes (e.g., excessive control or functionalization) and apply the appropriate remedy; do not simply pile more control functions into the congested office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Before centralizing control, consider necessity, duplication, time, and load
rubrics_metrics.description: When considering assignment of detailed control duties to a superimposed staff division, examine: (1) the necessity or non-necessity of control functions and their duplication of line controls; (2) the time required for performance of control functions; (3) the load of these functions on the officials performing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these points to decide whether central control will actually add value or simply create delays and bottlenecks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place paper-clearance control with knowledgeable line officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Control, insofar as it is exercised through clearance of papers, should be in the hands of superior line officers and their assistants who have a working knowledge of the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid having clerks or staff unfamiliar with subject-matter act as de facto controllers; unnecessary clearance steps should be abolished or restricted to matters meriting serious attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan timing and schedule: when and how long
rubrics_metrics.description: Design of plan includes setting up quantitative, qualitative, and functional relationships; it is necessary to plan when things will be done and how long they will take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The planner must follow through, spot needs for adjustment, and inform administrators whether work is proceeding orderly or corrective steps are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop techniques of exact observation and measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative analysts should develop techniques of exact observation and measurement to tell how much each unit can produce on a given budget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative knowledge is essential for judging output and budgeting; employ time studies, work records, diaries, inspections, and suitable measurement techniques fitted to the organization's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand time–cost relationships and account for motion delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitative planning: time required for an operation times the rate of pay equals the wage cost; total time for an administrative sequence is the sum of individual job-times plus aggregate motion delay; time accounting is necessary for cost accounting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include charges for materials, space, utilities; measure motion delay and incorporate allowances when estimating total cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish work units and standard times for tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing of work requires a work unit; in simple tasks the unit is easily derived (bricklayer measured by hundreds, roofer by square, etc.) and reduced to man-hours via standard time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For standardized manual and clerical tasks develop work units and standard times, and convert to man-hours for estimating, scheduling and budgeting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use records and inspection to estimate times for variable tasks; allow leeway
rubrics_metrics.description: When items vary in size and difficulty but general character is same, obtain average time values by inspecting work records, file copies, counting production, or keeping diaries; for highly variable or new jobs estimate by experience and allow leeway.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate work records and periodic stock-taking reduce uncertainty; inability to do stop-watch studies is not fatal if sufficient allowances for variation are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce individual and group workload estimates including motion delay
rubrics_metrics.description: Work load analysis produces load estimates for individuals (for distribution) and approximate times for performing each task; these may be compounded into group work load estimates and times for entire projects, including allowance for motion delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these estimates for scheduling, staffing, and budgetary planning; include periodic correction of initial tentative estimates as circumstances warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multi-dimensional analysis (function, unit, sequence; Loveridge questions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before setting time estimates get an all-round picture using analysis by function, by unit of organization, and by administrative sequence; consider Loveridge's questions (purpose/necessity, who, what and method, assignment, work load, coordination, timing, balance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine qualitative and quantitative analyses; enlist cooperation of persons whose work is studied to arrive at practical quantitative estimates.
